content: Camellia sinensis, commonly known as the tea plant, is the species from which tea leaves and leaf buds are harvested to produce various types of tea. It belongs to the genus Camellia, a group of flowering plants in the family Theaceae. The plant is the source of white tea, green tea, oolong tea, and black tea, all of which are derived from its leaves but processed differently to achieve varying levels of oxidation. Kukicha, or twig tea, is also made from Camellia sinensis, but it uses the twigs and stems instead of the leaves. The species name sinensis is Latin for Chinese, and the genus name Camellia honors Rev. Georg Kamel, a Czech Jesuit priest and botanist, though he neither discovered nor named the plant. The naming was done by Carl Linnaeus, the father of modern taxonomy, to recognize Kamel's contributions to science. Historically, the tea plant has also been referred to as Thea bohea, Thea sinensis, and Thea viridis. Camellia sinensis is native to mainland South and Southeast Asia but is now cultivated worldwide in tropical and subtropical regions. It is an evergreen shrub or small tree, typically pruned to a height of less than two meters when grown for its leaves. The plant has a strong taproot and produces flowers with 7 to 8 petals. Its seeds can be pressed to produce tea oil, a sweet cooking oil distinct from tea tree oil, which is an essential oil used for medicinal and cosmetic purposes. The leaves of Camellia sinensis range from 4 to 15 cm in length and 2 to 5 cm in width. Fresh leaves contain approximately 4% caffeine. Young, light green leaves, which have short white hairs on their undersides, are preferred for tea production, while older leaves are darker green. The chemical composition of the leaves varies with age, influencing the quality of the tea produced. Typically, the bud and the first two to three leaves are hand-picked for processing, with harvesting repeated every one to two weeks. The three most common types of tea—green, oolong, and black—are all made from the same plant. Green tea is steamed (Japanese method) or roasted (Chinese method) shortly after picking to prevent oxidation. Oolong tea undergoes partial oxidation, while black tea is fully oxidized, resulting in the darkest tea. White tea, a delicacy in the East now gaining popularity in the West, is made from the newest, still-folded shoots of leaves, often referred to as tea needles. Further distinctions in tea are based on leaf size (with younger, smaller leaves generally considered to produce higher-quality flavors) and the region of origin, similar to the classification of wine. Camellia sinensis is primarily cultivated in tropical and subtropical climates, requiring at least 50 inches of annual rainfall. However, it is commercially grown as far north as Cornwall in the UK. High-quality teas are often grown at elevations up to 1,500 meters, where slower plant growth enhances flavor. If left undisturbed, tea plants can grow into trees, but cultivated plants are pruned to waist height for easier harvesting. Two main varieties are used in tea production: the small-leaved Chinese variety (C. sinensis sinensis) and the large-leaved Assamese variety (C. sinensis assamica), the latter being primarily used for black tea. The Assamese variety, native to northeast India, Myanmar, Vietnam, and southern China, is a small tree with large leaves. In the wild, it can grow up to 20 meters tall but is pruned to waist height on tea estates. It thrives in lowland areas with high rainfall and good drainage but does not tolerate extreme temperatures. Discovered in 1823, it is one of the two original tea plants and is used to produce Assam and most Ceylon teas, which are known for their malty, earthy flavors, in contrast to the floral notes of the Chinese variety. The Chinese variety, native to southeast China, is a small-leaved bush with multiple stems that grows up to 3 meters tall. It was the first tea plant to be discovered, recorded, and used for tea production over 3,000 years ago. This variety produces some of the most popular teas. Another variety, sometimes referred to as Walden's Camellia, is found in Hong Kong and parts of China. The Cambodian variety, with leaves intermediate in size between the Assamese and Chinese varieties, is a small tree with several stems and is sometimes considered a hybrid of the two. The leaves of Camellia sinensis have been used in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) and other medical systems to treat conditions such as asthma, angina pectoris, peripheral vascular disease, and coronary artery disease. Tea extracts are being studied for their potential antibacterial properties, particularly in preserving processed organic food and treating persistent bacterial infections. Green tea leaves and extracts have demonstrated effectiveness against bacteria responsible for bad breath. Additionally, the tea component epicatechin gallate is being researched for its ability to reverse methicillin resistance in bacteria like Staphylococcus aureus in vitro. If confirmed, this could enhance the effectiveness of methicillin treatment against resistant bacterial strains when combined with tea extracts containing this compound.
